title: A Blank Key Holds the Kinase Shut

scenes.tts: What keeps a kinase off until cyclic AMP arrives? Protein kinase A reads cyclic AMP. At rest it is a complex of four subunits. Two are catalytic subunits, and each is a complete kinase. Two are regulatory subunits, which keep the catalytic ones off.
scenes.caption: What keeps a kinase off until cAMP arrives? Protein kinase A reads cAMP. At rest it is a complex of four subunits. Two are catalytic subunits, and each is a complete kinase. Two are regulatory subunits, which keep the catalytic ones off.
scenes.visual: One catalytic blob with 'off?'; then the four-subunit complex builds, labelled catalytic and regulatory, with OFF over the catalytic ones.
scenes.narration: What keeps a kinase off until cAMP arrives? Protein kinase A reads cAMP. At rest it is a complex of four subunits. Two are catalytic subunits, and each is a complete kinase. Two are regulatory subunits, which keep the catalytic ones off.

scenes.tts: The kinase phosphorylates a serine or threonine that lies close after a pair of arginines in its target. Each regulatory subunit carries a short stretch that looks like such a target. That stretch lies in the active site of the catalytic subunit, where a substrate would go.
scenes.visual: Zoom to one pair. A target strip (Arg Arg Ser/Thr) takes a phosphate. The regulatory subunit's tab looks like it and sits in the catalytic subunit's slot.
scenes.narration: The kinase phosphorylates a serine or threonine that lies close after a pair of arginines in its target. Each regulatory subunit carries a short stretch that looks like such a target. That stretch lies in the active site of the catalytic subunit, where a substrate would go.

scenes.tts: In type one regulatory subunits, the serine position holds a residue that cannot accept a phosphate. So the stretch fits, but it is never phosphorylated. It is called a pseudosubstrate. Think of a blank key left in a lock. It fits and will not turn, so no working key can get in.
scenes.caption: In type I regulatory subunits, the serine position holds a residue that cannot accept a phosphate. So the stretch fits, but it is never phosphorylated. It is called a pseudosubstrate. Think of a blank key left in a lock. It fits and will not turn, so no working key can get in.
scenes.visual: The stretch's last position becomes a red residue that refuses a phosphate; the tab is a blank key in a lock; a working target key is blocked.
scenes.narration: In type I regulatory subunits, the serine position holds a residue that cannot accept a phosphate. So the stretch fits, but it is never phosphorylated. It is called a pseudosubstrate. Think of a blank key left in a lock. It fits and will not turn, so no working key can get in.

scenes.tts: Each regulatory subunit has two binding sites for cyclic AMP, four in the whole complex. When cyclic AMP fills them, the subunit changes shape and lets go. In the classical model, the catalytic subunits come away free and begin phosphorylating targets. There is evidence that the kinase on an anchoring protein can act on nearby targets without fully coming apart. So the textbook picture may not hold everywhere. A kinase held shut by its own partner, until cyclic AMP fills the sites.

scenes.visual: Four cAMP sites fill, regulatory subunits change shape and release the tabs, catalytic subunits drift free and phosphorylate targets; hedge labels; the complex closes again.
